claim: Residues in the pore-domain can dramatically tune sensitivity to activators in TRPV1-3 channels.
source: We and others have shown that residues in the pore-domain can dramatically tune sensitivity to activators in TRPV1-3 channels (Jordt et al., 2000; Grandl et al., 2008; Grandl et al., 2010; Jara-Oseguera et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Eight additional positions in the pore domain are conserved in rTRPV2 and mTRPV3 channels but not in rTRPV1 channels.
source: We found eight additional positions in the pore domain that are conserved in rTRPV2 and mTRPV3 channels but not in rTRPV1 channels (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) – A552, V553, L555, and S557 in the S5 helix of rTRPV2 (S592, T593, V595, T597 in rTRPV1), D595 and A596 in the pore helix of rTRPV2 (S632, T633), Q613 above the selectivity filter in rTRPV2 (T650 in rTRPV1), and L623 in the S6 helix of rTRPV2 (I660 in rTRPV1).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The sensitivity to 2-APB was highly disrupted in rTRPV1-12M channels.
source: The sensitivity to 2-APB was highly disrupted in rTRPV2-12M channels (Figure 7A), with a concentration of 12 mM 2-APB producing a similar extent of activation as 50 µM 2-APB in WT rTRPV1 channels relative to 10 µM capsaicin. (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Sensitivity to CBD and the magnitude of the sensitization caused by CBD appeared to be minimally affected in rTRPV1-12M channels relative to WT rTRPV1.
source: In contrast to the heavily impaired sensitivity to 2-APB, sensitivity to CBD, and the magnitude of the sensitization caused by CBD appeared to be minimally affected relative to WT rTRPV1 (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and C

claim: rTRPV1-14M channels behaved very similarly to rTRPV1-12M channels.
source: Finally, we introduced two additional substitutions at the extracellular S6 loop (Y653L and D654R) of rTRPV1-12M channels, which are not conserved between rTRPV2, mTRPV3, and TRPV1 channels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and found that the resulting channels, rTRPV1-14M, behaved very similarly to rTRPV1-12M channels (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and C

claim: Differences in the amino acid sequence of the pore domain between the rTRPV2 and rTRPV1 channels are not responsible for the different sensitization strength caused by CBD binding in each of these two channels.
source: Together, our results establish that differences in the amino acid sequence of the pore domain between the rTRPV2 and rTRPV1 channels are not responsible for the different sensitization strength caused by CBD binding in each of these two channels.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data

claim: The determinants for sensitization strength must be located at other sites of the protein further from the CBD binding site(s).
source: These results also indicate that the determinants for sensitization strength must be located at other sites of the protein further from the CBD binding site(s).
evidence: Based on inference from mutagenesis data

claim: CBD sensitized all three channels (rTRPV1, rTRPV2, mTRPV3) to subsequent activation by 2-APB.
source: Despite the low efficacy of CBD relative to 2-APB as an agonist of rTRPV2, rTRPV1, and mTRPV3 channels, CBD sensitized all three channels to subsequent activation by 2-APB.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Sensitization by CBD in rTRPV2 and mTRPV3 channels was orders of magnitude stronger than in rTRPV1 channels.
source: However, sensitization in rTRPV2 and mTRPV3 channels was orders of magnitude stronger than in rTRPV1 channels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The cryo-EM structural data for the full-length rTRPV2 in the presence of CBD and 2-APB confirmed the location of the CBD binding site.
source: Our cryo-EM structural data for the full-length rTRPV2 in the presence of CBD and 2-APB confirmed the location of the CBD binding site (Pumroy et al., 2019; Pumroy et al., 2022) at the interface between the pore domain, the membrane and the S4-S5 linker helix (Figure 3), and identified a second location where CBD or other small molecules could possibly bind.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3 and citations

claim: The regions where CBD binds in rTRPV2 channels are highly conserved between TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 channels.
source: The regions where CBD binds in rTRPV2 channels are highly conserved between TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 channels (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and our mutagenesis results with rTRPV1 and rTRPV2 channels establish that the few residues that are not conserved between these channels are not determinant for the strength of the sensitization caused by CBD binding.
evidence: Based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The few residues that are not conserved between TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 channels are not determinant for the strength of the sensitization caused by CBD binding.
source: The regions where CBD binds in rTRPV2 channels are highly conserved between TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 channels (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and our mutagenesis results with rTRPV1 and rTRPV2 channels establish that the few residues that are not conserved between these channels are not determinant for the strength of the sensitization caused by CBD binding.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data

claim: CBD interacts at similar locations in TRPV1 and TRPV2 channels.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that CBD interacts at similar locations in TRPV1 and TRPV2 channels, and speculate that this may also apply to TRPV3 channels.
evidence: Based on inference from structural and mutagenesis data

claim: CBD may interact at similar locations in TRPV3 channels as in TRPV1 and TRPV2.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that CBD interacts at similar locations in TRPV1 and TRPV2 channels, and speculate that this may also apply to TRPV3 channels.
evidence: Based on speculation from structural and mutagenesis data

claim: The 2-APB binding sites proposed based on observations in TRPV3 and TRPV2 channel structures lack sequence conservation.
source: In contrast to the CBD site, the 2-APB binding sites proposed based on observations in TRPV3 (Singh et al., 2018b; Zubcevic et al., 2019) and TRPV2 (Pumroy et al., 2022; Su et al., 2023) channel structures lack sequence conservation, suggesting that the energetics of activation by 2-APB could be very different in TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 channels, and could even involve distinct regions in each channel.
evidence: Based on comparison of structures and sequence analysis

claim: The energetics of activation by 2-APB could be very different in TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 channels.
source: In contrast to the CBD site, the 2-APB binding sites proposed based on observations in TRPV3 (Singh et al., 2018b; Zubcevic et al., 2019) and TRPV2 (Pumroy et al., 2022; Su et al., 2023) channel structures lack sequence conservation, suggesting that the energetics of activation by 2-APB could be very different in TRPV1, TRPV2, and TRPV3 channels, and could even involve distinct regions in each channel.

claim: Binding of CBD in rTRPV2 channels favors rearrangements on multiple sites in the protein that contribute energetically to activation by 2-APB without directly influencing the open-to-closed equilibrium.
source: We hypothesize that binding of CBD in rTRPV2 channels favors rearrangements on multiple sites in the protein that contribute energetically to activation by 2-APB without directly influencing the open-to-closed equilibrium because CBD is such a low-efficacy agonist.
evidence: Based on speculation from experimental data

claim: Mutations at the site where CBD binds would significantly affect sensitivity to 2-APB by means of allosteric coupling.
source: Because binding of CBD sensitizes responses to 2-APB in rTRPV1 and rTRPV2 channels, albeit with different strength, it can be predicted that mutations at the site where CBD binds would significantly affect sensitivity to 2-APB by means of allosteric coupling.
evidence: Based on inference from sensitization data

claim: Each of the positions substituted in the mutagenesis study had a minor influence on the sensitivity of rTRPV1 and rTRPV2 channels to CBD and a stronger influence on the sensitivity to 2-APB.
source: Indeed, we found that each of the positions we substituted had a minor influence on the sensitivity of rTRPV1 and rTRPV2 channels to CBD and a stronger influence on the sensitivity to 2-APB; further, each of the rTRPV1 channel mutants we examined affected sensitivity to 2-APB more strongly than to capsaicin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Each of the rTRPV1 channel mutants examined affected sensitivity to 2-APB more strongly than to capsaicin.
source: Indeed, we found that each of the positions we substituted had a minor influence on the sensitivity of rTRPV1 and rTRPV2 channels to CBD and a stronger influence on the sensitivity to 2-APB; further, each of the rTRPV1 channel mutants we examined affected sensitivity to 2-APB more strongly than to capsaicin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The apparent affinity for 2-APB and sensitization by CBD are not strictly coupled in rTRPV1 channels.
source: Our mutagenesis results, however, show that the apparent affinity for 2-APB and sensitization by CBD are not strictly coupled in rTRPV1 channels: mutant M572V had an EC50 for 2-APB that is similar in magnitude to WT rTRPV2 channels, and yet sensitization by CBD was completely absent, whereas the apparent 2-APB affinity for the triple mutant rTRPV1-M572V+C578L+M581L was so low that an EC50 could not be determined, and yet responses to 2-APB were sensitized by CBD to the same extent as in WT rTRPV1 channels (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 6E–G

claim: The ensembles of conformational channel states stabilized by distinct agonists and allosteric modulators differ from each other at multiple significant locations throughout the protein.
source: Observations like this suggest a framework of TRPV channel function where the ensembles of conformational channel states stabilized by distinct agonists and allosteric modulators differ from each other at multiple significant locations throughout the protein, and that these differences, which could involve relatively subtle structural rearrangements, ultimately determine how the ensemble will respond to further challenges.
evidence: Based on inference from mutagenesis and functional data

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H

claim: The ensemble of conformations adopted by the rTRPV2 channel when bound to CBD has energetically significant differences from the set of conformations that predominate after channels become sensitized by a strong stimulation with 2-APB.
source: This large difference suggests that the ensemble of conformations adopted by the rTRPV2 channel when bound to CBD must have energetically significant differences from the set of conformations that predominate after channels become sensitized by a strong stimulation with 2-APB.
evidence: Based on inference from sensitization data

claim: Sensitization by extreme heat increases the apparent affinity of rTRPV2 channels for 2-APB to a similar extent as CBD does.
source: Sensitization by extreme heat increases the apparent affinity of rTRPV2 channels for 2-APB to a similar extent as CBD does, and also results in noticeable channel activity at ~40°C (Liu and Qin, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The structural ensemble of heat-sensitized rTRPV2 channels bears significant differences at the energetic level from that of CBD-bound channels at temperatures below 40°C.
source: We did not detect rTPRV2 channel activity at ~40°C in the presence of CBD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that CBD binding is not strongly coupled to heat activation, and suggesting that the structural ensemble of heat-sensitized channels also bears significant differences at the energetic level from that of CBD-bound channels at temperatures below 40°C.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2
